result.markdown: # String ![](/images/string_bubble.png){style="width:200px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 5px white solid" fig-align="center"} __Strings__ are text. They can be modified with R in ways you would normally want to modify text. They are called __strings__ as they are strings of characters. __Strings__ are flanked by quote marks. Double quotes (`""`) are preferred but single quotes can also be used (`''`). Below are some examples to get some practice with __strings__. ## Text ![](/images/text_icon.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 0px white solid" fig-align="center"} A __string object__ can consist of a string containing one __character__: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #String one_character_string <- "A" one_character_string ``` ::: A __string object__ can consist of a string containing multiple __characters__: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} word_string <- "alphabet" word_string ``` ::: A __string__ can contain all the different characters and any number of them. The only exception is that if you try to put a double quote in your string it will cause an issue. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} long_string <- "Strings can be long and contain more than letters. \\.(" long_string ``` ::: ## Numbers ![](/images/number_text.png){style="width:250px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 0px white solid" fig-align="center"} A __string__ doesn't need letters, it can consist of only numbers. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} number_string <- "1066" number_string class(number_string) ``` ::: ::: {.callout-note} The terms __string__ and __character__ can be used interchangeably. ::: ## String conversion ![](/images/string_conversion.png){style="width:400px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 0px white solid" fig-align="center"} You can convert a __numeric__ to a __string/character__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} number <- 1066 numeric_to_string <- as.character(number) numeric_to_string class(numeric_to_string) ``` ::: An appropriate __string__ can be converted to a __numeric__. This is useful as mathematical __operators__ will not work with __strings__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #will get an error as strings and maths don't mix "6" - 3 #will work as maths and numerics work as.numeric("6") - 4 #Below will not work as only strings containing numbers can be converted to numeric as.numeric("not_a_number_12") ``` ::: ## Logical comparisons ![](/images/trueorfalse.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 0px white solid" fig-align="center"} You can use certain __logical operators__ to compare __strings__. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # "character" the same as "character" "character" == "character" #"1066" not the same as "character" "1066" != "character" #"numeric" the same as "string" "numeric" == "string" ``` ::: ## Combining strings ![](/images/combine_icon.png){style="width:150px; background: white; border-radius:5px; border: 5px white solid" fig-align="center"} The __paste() function__ is very useful to combine two or more __strings__ into one. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} paste("The following is a string:", long_string) paste(number_string, "and the", word_string) #By default paste will put a space (sep = " ") between each string you provide #You can use the sep option to specify your own paste("However", " this is separated by a comma", sep = ",") #Or you can make it so there is no separator paste("no separator",numeric_to_string, sep = "") #Alternatively you can use paste0() #Where there is no separator by default (sep ="") paste0("no separator",numeric_to_string) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ```{=html} ``` ::: :::
